blocks.text: The rates of different chemical reactions differ greatly: the reaction of NaCl with AgNO3 is very fast, the hydrolysis of an ester proceeds at a moderate rate, and the rusting of iron is slow. An explosion is a swift reaction over in a fraction of a second, while rusting may take days or months. Reaction kinetics is the study of the rates of chemical reactions, including the experimental methods for measuring rates, orders and mechanisms. Rates and their control are often important in industry, where they may decide whether a reaction can be used economically, so it matters to discover the conditions under which a reaction proceeds most economically.

Collision theory explains how reactions occur. For a chemical reaction to take place, the particles of the reactants, atoms, ions or molecules, must form a homogeneous mixture and collide with one another. The collisions may be effective or ineffective depending on the energy of the colliding particles: effective collisions give products, otherwise the particles just bounce back. Effective collisions take place only when the colliding particles possess a certain amount of energy and approach each other with the proper orientation.

blocks.title: Activation energy
blocks.text: The minimum amount of energy required for an effective collision between the reacting species is called the activation energy. Most reactions are slow, showing that not all collisions are equally effective.

The process can be understood from a graph of potential energy against the path of reaction. If a collision is effective the molecules flying apart are chemically different; otherwise the same molecules bounce back. The reactants reach the peak of the curve to form the activated complex, and only the colliding molecules with the proper activation energy can climb the hill and give products.
